L0@P0: ON UNIQUE FACTORIZATION DOMAINS
L1@P0: BY
L2@P0: PIERRE SAMUEL
L3@P0: A unique factorization domain (or UFD) is an integral domain in which
L4@P0: every element 0 is, in an essentially unique way (i.e., up to units), a product
L5@P0: of irreducible ones. In spite of the simplicity of this notion, many problems
L6@P0: concerning it have remained open for many years. For example the fact that
L7@P0: every regular local ring is a UFD has been coniectured in the early 40’s, many
L8@P0: partial results in this direction have been proved, but the general case has
L9@P0: been settled only in 1959 by M. Auslander and D. Buchsbaum [1]. Another
L10@P0: open question was as to whether a power series ring over a UFD is a UFD;
L11@P0: W. Krull studied it in a paper of 1938, and termed the answer "doubtful"
L12@P0: ("zweifelhaft") [3]; we prove here that the answer to this question is negative.

L23: 【8†Lemma 10.40.4.】 Let $R \to S$ be a flat ring map. Let $M$ be an $R$-module and $m \in M$. Then $\text{Ann}_ R(m) S = \text{Ann}_ S(m \otimes 1)$. If $M$ is a finite $R$-module, then $\text{Ann}_ R(M) S = \text{Ann}_ S(M \otimes _ R S)$.

L132@P2: (I : I) will contain R. This order is called the multiplicator ring of I. A fractional ideal I
L133@P2: is called invertible if I(S : I) = S, where S is the multiplicator ring of I.
L134@P2: An order S is called Gorenstein if every fractional ideal with multiplicator ring S is invertible, or equivalently if S
L135@P2: t
L136@P2: is an invertible ideal, see [BL94, Proposition 2.7]. Examples
L137@P2: of Gorenstein orders are OK and the monogenic order R = Z[x]/(f ), see [BL94, Example
L138@P2: 2.8]. An order R is called Bass if every over-order of R is Gorenstein. Since in this paper
L139@P2: we will extensively use the properties of Bass orders we will list here other equivalent
L140@P2: definitions.
L141@P2: Proposition 2.1. Let R be an order. The following are equivalent:
L142@P2: • R is Bass (every over-order is Gorenstein);
L143@P2: • every fractional R-ideal can be generated by 2 elements;
L144@P2: • R is a cyclic index order, that is, the finite R-module OK /R is cyclic.
